scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8879: Users in both pods report that no internal portal
loads by NAME anymore -- web0.local through web3.local all fail with
name-resolution errors. Loading a portal directly by its IP address (e.g.
http://10.200.0.3) still works, and pings to 10.200.0.2 succeed. Diagnose.

injection.action: stop the BIND (named) DNS service on dns_server

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: dns_server BIND (named) DNS service
Mechanism: the named daemon on dns_server (10.200.0.2) has been killed, so
  nothing answers on port 53 and every *.local lookup from the pods times
  out -- which is why the portals fail by name. Everything else is healthy:
  the host 10.200.0.2 itself is up and pingable, the OSPF path works, and
  the web servers keep serving HTTP (portals load when addressed by IP).
  The symptom is purely dead name resolution.
Localization: dns_server
Root cause: named not running on dns_server (port 53 closed)
Fix: `systemctl start named` on dns_server
scenario.fix_spec:
Restart the BIND DNS service on dns_server (e.g. `systemctl start named`).
Once named is answering again, web0.local..web3.local resolve to their
10.200.0.x addresses and the portals load by name. The web servers and the
network need no change.
scoring_axes: must-identify-component: BIND/named DNS service down (name resolution dead, port 53 closed)
bonus-rules-out-network: notes 10.200.0.2 is reachable and portals load by IP, so the network and web servers are healthy -- only resolution is broken

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: the DNS service on dns_server (BIND/named). Mechanism: All clients are configured to use 10.200.0.2 as their resolver, so when the DNS daemon is not listening on port 53, queries fail immediately with “connection refused.” That produces name-resolution errors for web0.local–web3.local, while direct access by IP continues to work because general IP routing is unaffected.

Localization: On dns_server, no process is listening on port 53 (netstat/ss shows no 53 listener). Systemd reports the DNS daemon is not running: “named.service … Active: inactive (dead)” and “bind9.service … Active: inactive (dead).” From the clients host_1_1_1_1 and host_2_1_1_1, resolv.conf points to nameserver 10.200.0.2, and nslookup to 10.200.0.2 returns “connection refused,” confirming reachability to the host but no DNS service bound to the port. Network connectivity is otherwise healthy (pings succeed across the topology).

Root cause: The BIND/named DNS service on dns_server is stopped, leaving no listener on UDP/TCP 53.

Corrective fix: Restart and enable the DNS service on dns_server (e.g., systemctl restart named && systemctl enable named), then verify it is listening on :53 and responding to queries. If it fails to start, run named-checkconf and review journalctl -u named for configuration errors; correct any zone or config issues and restart. After recovery, confirm clients can resolve web0.local–web3.local and consider adding monitoring/alerts on the DNS service.

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly identifies and localizes the fault to dns_server (BIND/named) with evidence of no listener on port 53.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly identifies the BIND/named DNS service on dns_server as stopped, notes no listener on UDP/TCP port 53 and resulting name-resolution failures.

per_axis.axis: bonus-rules-out-network: notes 10.200.0.2 is reachable and portals load by IP, so the network and web servers are healthy -- only resolution is broken
per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly states 10.200.0.2 is reachable (nslookup returns connection refused, pings succeed) and portals load by IP, thereby ruling out network or web-server failures and isolating the problem to name resolution.
Recommends restarting/enabling the named service and verifying it listens/responds on port 53, which matches the expected remediation.

The agent's observations (clients point to 10.200.0.2, nslookup returned 'connection refused', netstat/ss had no :53 listener, and systemctl shows named inactive) directly support its conclusion that the DNS daemon is stopped; the causal steps are logical. One minor gap: an explicit HTTP-by-IP check isn't shown in the log, but reachability data implies networking is otherwise healthy.
